title: One file to ship: bundling with esbuild

story: The harness is the program that runs inside every one of Nova's machines: it reads the task, starts the Claude session, runs the checks and saves checkpoints. The machines start from one prepared image, and nothing is installed on them while a run is going. The first time someone put the harness into the image, they copied tsc's dist/ folder. The first run crashed on line one with Cannot find package 'zod', because zod lived in node_modules on the build machine, and nobody copied node_modules.

The second attempt copied node_modules too: hundreds of megabytes, tens of thousands of files, and one package at a different version from the one the tests had used, because the image ran its own npm install. Now nobody could say exactly which code was running on Nova's machines.
hook.question: How do I ship a Node program to a machine as one file that needs nothing but Node itself, and how do I prove that nothing is missing before it ever reaches the machine?

read.h: Built code still needs its packages
p: In lesson p1-1, tsc turned src/main.ts into dist/main.js, and a service image ran that file. But tsc only translates your own files. Every import of a package, such as import { z } from "zod", stays an import, and at run time Node looks for zod in a node_modules folder next to the code. For a service in a Docker image that is fine, because the image installs node_modules from the lockfile (lesson p1-8).

The harness is different. It runs directly on the machine, next to the product's own tools, and we want exactly one tested thing there. That is what a bundler gives you. It starts at your entry file, follows every import, including the ones into node_modules, and writes all of it into one file. The file needs nothing but Node: no node_modules, no package.json, no install. It is also one version: the same file runs on the machine and in the benchmark that scores the agent, so a score describes exactly what ships.

notes.text: process.argv[0] is node and [1] the script, so the real arguments start at index 2.
Exit code 2 is the usual answer to wrong usage, so scripts can tell it apart from a failed check (1).
The zod schema from lesson p1-5. zod goes into the bundle with it.
Sets the exit code but lets Node finish writing the output first.

read.see:
$ cp dist/unbundled.mjs ~/academy-labs/p1-7-empty/ && node ~/academy-labs/p1-7-empty/unbundled.mjs check scope.json
Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find package 'zod' imported from …/p1-7-empty/unbundled.mjs

read.h: The esbuild command, flag by flag
p: esbuild is a bundler written in Go, and it is very fast: a bundle like ours takes a few milliseconds. For a Node program you tell it five things, and each flag changes what the file can do on the machine. --bundle pulls every import into the file. --platform=node leaves Node's own modules, such as node:fs, as imports, because Node provides them. --format=esm writes an ES module, and the .mjs ending tells Node so without a package.json. --target=node24 writes syntax Node 24 runs as it is.

The last flag adds a banner, a line of text at the very top of the file. #!/usr/bin/env node is a shebang: when you run the file as a command, the operating system reads that first line and starts node with the file. Together with chmod +x, which marks the file as executable, it turns lab-worker.mjs into a command you can type like git or ls.

notes.text: Follow every import, packages included, and put it all in one file.
Keep node: built-ins as imports instead of trying to bundle them.
Write syntax the machine's Node runs without changes.
The shebang must be the very first line of the file.
One output file. dist/ is never committed.

read.h: Prove it in an empty folder
p: A bundle that works in your project folder proves little, because your node_modules is right there and Node will happily find anything the bundle missed. The real test is to copy the file, alone, into a folder with nothing else in it, and run it there. If it still works, the bundle is complete. That is exactly the situation on Nova's machine.
Check the exit codes while you are there, because the code that starts the harness reads them: 0 for a good scope, 1 for a bad one, 2 for wrong usage.
read.see:
$ ls
lab-worker.mjs  scope.json
$ ./lab-worker.mjs check scope.json
ok: RhinoHealth/fcp nova/RH-1234
$ ./lab-worker.mjs; echo "exit $?"
usage: lab-worker check <scope.json>
exit 2

read.h: When a package still wants require
p: Many packages on npm are still written as CommonJS, the older module style that loads other modules with require(). Inside an ES module bundle there is no require, so esbuild leaves a small stand-in that throws when it is called. The trap is when: the build succeeds, and the error appears only when that line runs, which for the harness means on Nova's machine. The yaml package, which the harness uses to read settings and charters, is one of them.

The fix is a second banner line that creates a real require for the bundle with createRequire from node:module. In the real release build the shebang and this line go into one banner, shebang first. And the lesson from the previous section applies again: run the bundle, not only build it.

code.text:
npx esbuild src/charter.ts --bundle --platform=node --format=esm --outfile=dist/charter.mjs
node dist/charter.mjs
npx esbuild src/charter.ts --bundle --platform=node --format=esm --outfile=dist/charter.mjs \
  --banner:js='import { createRequire } from "node:module"; const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);'
node dist/charter.mjs

notes.text: Fails only now: Error: Dynamic require of "process" is not supported.
Gives the bundle a real require that can load Node's built-in modules.
Prints: charter for sean on red_main.

deeper.h: Go deeper: from one file to a release on the machine
p: A GitHub release is a git tag with files attached to it, called assets. The platform's release job bundles the harness into nova-worker.mjs, packs it with its prompts and settings into a .tgz file, and attaches that to a release with a command like gh release create v1.4.0 ai-agents-harness-1.4.0.tgz. An asset cannot change after it is published, so a version number always means the same bytes.

The nightly job that builds the machine image downloads that asset (gh release download does the same by hand), unpacks it into a fixed folder and links /usr/local/bin/nova-worker to the file. Nothing is installed. The harness also loads the Claude Agent SDK from its entry for bundled programs, @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk/core, and points it at the claude binary pinned in the image, so the bundle carries the code and the image carries the binary that was tested.

lab.title: Bundle a small worker and run it where nothing is installed
needs: About 20 MB of disk for zod, yaml and esbuild
lab.goal: See unbundled code fail without node_modules, bundle it into one executable file that runs from an empty folder, and fix a package that needs require.

guess.q: You build src/cli.ts without --bundle and copy the output, alone, into an empty folder. It imports zod. What happens when you run it there?

options.text: It works, because the build already turned zod into JavaScript.
options.why: Without --bundle only your own file is translated. The import of zod stays an import, and Node goes looking for it.

options.text: It fails with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND: Cannot find package 'zod'.
options.why: Node looks for zod in a node_modules folder next to the file, and the empty folder has none. That is the crash from the story.

options.text: Node downloads zod from npm the first time it is needed.
options.why: Node never installs anything by itself. And Nova's machines cannot reach the public npm registry anyway.

follow.say: Make the project with two real dependencies, zod and yaml, and esbuild as a dev tool. Also make the empty folder you will test in.
follow.do: mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/p1-7/src ~/academy-labs/p1-7-empty && cd ~/academy-labs/p1-7 && npm init -y > /dev/null && npm pkg set type=module && npm install --save-exact zod@4.6.7 yaml@2.8.1 > /dev/null && npm install -D --save-exact tsx@4.20.3 @types/node@24.12.2 esbuild@0.25.10 > /dev/null && echo ready

follow.say: Write the small worker and a scope file, and run it with tsx first.
Build it without --bundle, the way tsc would, and run the result from the empty folder.
follow.do: npx esbuild src/cli.ts --platform=node --format=esm --outfile=dist/unbundled.mjs && cp dist/unbundled.mjs scope.json ../p1-7-empty/ && node ../p1-7-empty/unbundled.mjs check scope.json

Make it executable, copy it alone into the empty folder, and run it there as a command, with a good scope and with no arguments.
follow.do: head -1 dist/lab-worker.mjs && chmod +x dist/lab-worker.mjs && cp dist/lab-worker.mjs ../p1-7-empty/ && cd ../p1-7-empty && ./lab-worker.mjs check scope.json; ./lab-worker.mjs; echo "exit $?"; cd ../p1-7

lab.build: Ship the worker the way a release does. First give it a version subcommand: add declare const VERSION: string; to src/cli.ts and print VERSION when the command is version. Bundle it with the same five flags plus --define:VERSION='"0.1.0"', which tells esbuild to replace VERSION with that text. Then pack it the way the release job does, tar -czf dist/lab-worker-v0.1.0.tgz -C dist lab-worker.mjs, unpack the tarball into a new folder ~/academy-labs/p1-7-release, and run both lab-worker.mjs version and lab-worker.mjs check from there.
checks: The unbundled file failed in the empty folder with Cannot find package 'zod'.
The bundle is about 740 kB, starts with #!/usr/bin/env node, and runs as ./lab-worker.mjs from the empty folder.
Running it with no arguments prints the usage line and exit 2.
The yaml bundle failed with Dynamic require only when it ran, and worked with the createRequire banner.
From ~/academy-labs/p1-7-release, lab-worker.mjs version prints 0.1.0 and lab-worker.mjs check prints ok.

solution.text:
// src/cli.ts: two additions
declare const VERSION: string;   // esbuild replaces it at build time

if (command === "version") {     // right after reading command and file
  console.log(VERSION);
  process.exit(0);
}

# terminal
npx esbuild src/cli.ts --bundle --platform=node --format=esm --target=node24 \
  --banner:js='#!/usr/bin/env node' --define:VERSION='"0.1.0"' --outfile=dist/lab-worker.mjs
chmod +x dist/lab-worker.mjs
tar -czf dist/lab-worker-v0.1.0.tgz -C dist lab-worker.mjs
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/p1-7-release && tar -xzf dist/lab-worker-v0.1.0.tgz -C ~/academy-labs/p1-7-release
~/academy-labs/p1-7-release/lab-worker.mjs version          # 0.1.0
~/academy-labs/p1-7-release/lab-worker.mjs check scope.json # ok: RhinoHealth/fcp nova/RH-1234

lab.fix: To make the release bundle smaller, a teammate added --external:zod to the esbuild command, which tells esbuild to leave zod out of the bundle and keep it as an import. The file drops from about 740 kB to under one kilobyte and still works in the project folder, so the pull request looks great. Make the same change, run the bundle from the project folder and then from the empty folder, and explain why the second run is the one that tells the truth about Nova's machine.
explain: Why does the harness ship as one bundled file while the services ship as images with node_modules?
What does each of the five esbuild flags do, and which one makes ./lab-worker.mjs work as a command?
Why do we run a bundle from an empty folder, and why did the yaml problem appear only at run time?
lab.done: lab-worker.mjs, unpacked from your tarball into a fresh folder, prints 0.1.0 for version and ok for the scope.

check.q: The bundle works when you run it inside your project folder. Why is that not enough proof?

options.text: Because esbuild only checks syntax, not imports
options.why: esbuild does follow imports. The issue is what Node can find when the file runs, not what esbuild checked.

options.text: Because the project's node_modules is right there, so Node finds anything the bundle left out
options.why: Only an empty folder, like Nova's machine, shows whether the file really carries everything it needs.

options.text: Because a bundle only runs on the Node version that built it
options.why: --target controls the syntax, and Node 24 runs the bundle anywhere. The danger is a missing package, not the version.

check.q: A bundle that uses the yaml package builds without a warning, and on the machine it fails with Dynamic require of "process" is not supported. What is going on?

options.text: yaml is CommonJS and calls require, which does not exist in an ES module bundle, so esbuild's stand-in throws when the line runs
options.why: The fix is a banner line that creates a real require with createRequire(import.meta.url), and the habit is to run the bundle, not only build it.

options.text: The machine is missing the yaml package
options.why: yaml is inside the bundle. The problem is how yaml loads Node's own modules, not whether yaml is there.

options.text: --platform=node was forgotten, so Node built-ins are unavailable
options.why: With the wrong platform the build itself would complain about node: imports. This build was clean.

check.q: What does the first line #!/usr/bin/env node do in the bundled file?

options.text: It tells esbuild which Node version to target
options.why: That is --target. The shebang is for the operating system, not for esbuild.

options.text: It is a comment that Node prints when the program starts
options.why: Node skips the line. Its job is done before Node even starts.

options.text: It tells the operating system to start node with this file when you run the file as a command
options.why: With chmod +x and the shebang, ./lab-worker.mjs works like any command, which is how the image links /usr/local/bin/nova-worker to the bundle.

p: The platform's release-harness workflow bundles harness/ with esbuild into one file, nova-worker.mjs, with the shared package and every dependency inside and #!/usr/bin/env node on top. It packs that file with the harness's workflows, prompts and protected-paths settings into ai-agents-harness-<version>.tgz and attaches it to a GitHub release. The nightly Packer build of the machine image downloads that asset, unpacks it into /opt/ai-agents/harness and links /usr/local/bin/nova-worker, with nothing to install.

The harness imports the Agent SDK from @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk/core, the SDK's documented entry for bundled apps, and passes pathToClaudeCodeExecutable so the SDK runs the claude binary pinned in the image. The benchmark that scores Nova runs the same tarball, so a score describes exactly the file that ships.

tickets.why: release-harness.yml bundles harness/ with esbuild into nova-worker.mjs and attaches the tarball to a release.
The image build downloads the release asset, unpacks it and links /usr/local/bin/nova-worker.
The harness imports the SDK from /core and points it at the pinned claude binary.
The benchmark's Nova adapter runs the same tarball inside its task container.

words.plain: One file that holds your code and every package it imports, so it runs with nothing but Node.
A very fast bundler. Flags choose the platform, the module format and the syntax target.
A first line such as #!/usr/bin/env node that tells the operating system which program runs the file.
Text that esbuild puts at the very top of the output file.
The older Node module style with require() and module.exports. Some packages still use it.
A file attached to a GitHub release. Once published it does not change, so a version means the same bytes.

review.q: From memory: the esbuild command that turns src/cli.ts into one executable ES module for Node 24.
review.a: npx esbuild src/cli.ts --bundle --platform=node --format=esm --target=node24 --banner:js='#!/usr/bin/env node' --outfile=dist/lab-worker.mjs, then chmod +x.

review.q: A teammate asks why the harness is not a Docker image like the broker. What do you answer?
review.a: The harness runs directly on Nova's machine next to the product's tools, so it ships as one file that needs only Node, built once and tested once. The same file runs in the benchmark, and the image unpacks it with nothing to install.

remember: Bundle a program that runs on a machine into one ES module file with a shebang, prove it from an empty folder, and ship that exact file as a release.
